items.title: Mortgage and Loan Insurance Programs Under the National Housing Act-Debenture Interest Rates
items.summary: This notice announces changes in the interest rates to be paid on debentures issued with respect to a loan or mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration under the provisions of the National Housing Act (the Act). The interest rate for debentures issued under Section 221(g)(4) of the Act during the 6-month period beginning January 1, 2026, is 4 percent. The interest rate for debentures issued under any other provision of the Act is the rate in effect on the date that the commitment to insure the loan or mortgage was issued, or the date that the loan or mortgage was endorsed (or initially endorsed if there are two or more endorsements) for insurance, whichever rate is higher. The interest rate for debentures issued under these other provisions with respect to a loan or mortgage committed or endorsed during the 6-month period beginning January 1, 2026, is 4\3/4\ percent.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Health Deficiencies (08/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: Three years of nursing home health citations, one row per citation with scope, severity, current status and correction date, refreshed on 08/01/26 and untouched by monitored publishers.
story_ideas.consumer: Before you tour a facility, pull its citation history and look at two columns most families skip: scope and severity, and whether the citation is still open or was corrected. Ask the administrator directly about anything from the last three years that has not been closed out, and ask what changed afterward.
story_ideas.b2b: The refresh resets the comparison baseline for every operator in a market. Ownership groups can benchmark their citation profile against county and state peers and anticipate which tags referral sources and Medicaid managed care plans will screen on.
story_ideas.note: State and county detail supports a 50-state table and a county map. Coverage state is a confirmed gap.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Penalties (08/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: The file of fines and payment denials received by nursing homes over the last three years was refreshed on 08/01/26.
story_ideas.consumer: A fine is a harder fact than a star rating. Check whether the home you are considering has been fined or had Medicare payment denied in the last three years, and if it has, ask what the money was for and what the facility did in response.
story_ideas.b2b: Penalty history travels with a building through a sale. Pair the penalties file with the ownership file to see which portfolios carry concentrated enforcement exposure heading into a financing or acquisition conversation.
story_ideas.note: Chartable at state level. No monitored publisher matched it.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Ownership (08/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: Ownership information for every currently active nursing home, refreshed 08/01/26, sits alongside the citation and penalty files that can now be joined to it.
story_ideas.consumer: The name over the door often is not the company running the building. Look up who actually owns the home, then check whether that owner's other facilities in your state carry citations or fines.
story_ideas.b2b: Joining ownership to penalties and deficiencies produces the chain-level view operators rarely publish about themselves, and it is the analysis referral partners, lenders and state agencies increasingly want.
story_ideas.note: Strong original-analysis play; supports state concentration rankings. Confirmed gap.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Provider Information (08/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: The file behind the Five-Star Rating System, including certified beds, quality measure scores and staffing, was refreshed 08/01/26 with one row per nursing home.
story_ideas.consumer: Stars compress a lot of detail. Open the underlying numbers for the homes on your shortlist and compare certified beds and staffing side by side, then ask each one how many staff are on the floor overnight and on weekends.
story_ideas.b2b: Staffing figures inside this file are the ones payers, surveyors and families will cite back to operators all year. Knowing where a building sits against its state distribution is a recruiting and rate-negotiation input, not just a compliance one.
story_ideas.note: National, state and county cuts available; pairs naturally with the BLS nursing care employment series.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Fire Safety Deficiencies (08/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: Three years of nursing home fire safety citations, refreshed 08/01/26 and separately reported from health citations, which most consumer comparisons never surface.
story_ideas.consumer: Fire safety citations are listed apart from health citations, so a home can look clean on one list and not the other. Check both, and ask when the last fire safety inspection happened and whether anything is still open.
story_ideas.b2b: Life safety code findings are a distinct capital problem from clinical findings. The refreshed file lets operators and their capital partners see which markets carry the heaviest remediation load.
story_ideas.note: Rarely covered angle with clear local-market variation. Confirmed gap.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Hospice care - State and National CAHPS Hospice Survey Data (08/07/26)
story_ideas.hook: State and national average scores from the CAHPS Hospice Survey of Medicare-certified providers were refreshed on 08/07/26, anchoring a hospice cluster of nine items with no monitored coverage at all.
story_ideas.consumer: Hospice choice is usually made in a hurry. Look up how your state's hospice providers score on the family survey before you need one, and ask any agency you are offered how it compares to the state average.
story_ideas.b2b: Publicly comparable state averages sharpen the competitive picture for hospice operators and for the health systems and nursing homes that steer referrals to them.
story_ideas.note: The palliative and hospice cluster is the run's most internally coherent, at 0.457 cohesion across two sources, with all nine items unmatched.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Home health care services employment, August 2026 — 1,896.40 thousands of jobs (+5.0% year over year)
story_ideas.hook: Home health employment grew 5.0% year over year while nursing care facilities grew 2.1%, and home health average hourly earnings reached $28.04 in July 2026, up 2.0%.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are weighing home care against a facility, the labor market is moving toward home care. When you interview an agency, ask what it pays aides, how it has handled turnover in the last year, and who covers a shift when your regular aide is out.
story_ideas.b2b: A 5.0% employment gain against 2.1% in nursing facilities is a competition-for-labor story, and $28.04 an hour in home health against $25.65 in assisted living and continuing care sets the wage floor operators are hiring against.
story_ideas.note: Two clean national time series that chart well together; both are confirmed gaps.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Employment level, 65 years and over, August 2026 — 11,753 thousands of people (+2.1% year over year)
story_ideas.hook: Nearly 11.8 million people aged 65 and over were employed in August 2026, up 2.1% year over year, while medical care CPI rose 1.7% in July 2026.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are working past 65 or planning to, compare what another year of earnings does for you against what you are spending on medical care, which rose 1.7% over the year on the federal index. Check how continued work interacts with your benefits before you commit to a schedule.
story_ideas.b2b: Older workers are a labor pool senior living and home care operators recruit from and compete with. The growth rate matters for staffing plans that assume retirement-age attrition.
story_ideas.note: National only, but pairs with the medical care CPI series for a cost-versus-earnings chart.

story_ideas.title: Fair Market Rents for the Housing Choice Voucher Program and Other Programs, Fiscal Year 2027 (09/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: HUD published the FY 2027 fair market rents on 09/01/26, with the methods used to calculate them and the procedure for public housing agencies to request reevaluations.
story_ideas.consumer: If you rent with a voucher, the payment standard behind your rent is being reset effective October 1. Find your area's new figure and ask your housing agency what it means for your share of the rent next year.
story_ideas.b2b: Affordable senior housing operators and the agencies that fund them work off these numbers directly, and the reevaluation procedure is a live lever for markets where the published figure understates local rents.
story_ideas.note: Localizable to every FMR area; housing was one of two rising topics this run.

story_ideas.title: Housing Trust Fund: Fiscal Year 2026 Allocation Notice (09/04/26)
story_ideas.hook: HUD's FY 2026 Housing Trust Fund allocation notice, published 09/04/26, is the newest item in the run and names the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, American Samoa, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands among eligible grantees.
story_ideas.consumer: Housing Trust Fund money flows through your state to build and preserve rental housing. If you are on a waiting list for affordable senior housing, ask your state housing agency how it is programming this year's allocation.
story_ideas.b2b: Nonprofit developers building affordable senior housing plan against this notice. The allocation table is the starting point for the next application cycle.
story_ideas.note: Published the day of the run and unmatched; strongest fit for a state-by-state allocation table.

story_ideas.title: Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services for Older Adults: A Primer (08/20/26)
story_ideas.hook: Justice in Aging published a primer on 08/20/26 explaining how Medicaid HCBS help older adults with disabilities live independently and the policy gaps that limit access.
story_ideas.consumer: If staying at home is the goal, HCBS is the program that pays for it, and access depends on rules that vary. Ask your state Medicaid agency or Area Agency on Aging what services are covered, whether there is a waiting list, and what the financial eligibility test actually counts.
story_ideas.b2b: Home and community-based services are both the competitive alternative to facility care and a growth line for providers. The primer's account of access limits maps to where demand exists but funded capacity does not.
story_ideas.note: Not localizable on its own, but it frames the whole long-term care cluster and gives the CMS facility data its policy counterweight.

story_ideas.title: 5 Questions and Answers About Medicaid and Provider Taxes (08/20/26)
story_ideas.hook: KFF used its 2025-2026 survey of Medicaid directors and a proposed rule on provider taxes to describe how the rules are changing under the 2025 reconciliation law and which states each change may affect.
story_ideas.consumer: Provider taxes are one of the ways your state pays for nursing home and home care coverage. If your state's arrangement is changing, that is worth watching in the budget debate that decides eligibility and services where you live.
story_ideas.b2b: Provider tax structures underpin Medicaid rates. Operators need to know which of the changes described apply in their states and how far out the rate consequences run.
story_ideas.note: Sits in the Medicare and Medicaid cluster, which does not cohere; treat it as its own lead rather than part of a package.

trends_raw: Volume held essentially flat, 169 evidence candidates against 170 on 09/03/26, and nothing surfaced for the first time in this run. That makes it a consolidation day rather than a news day, and the interesting movement is in shape rather than size. Housing and financial security each gained an item, driven by federal register activity: fair market rents for FY 2027 on 09/01/26, the Housing Trust Fund FY 2026 allocation notice on 09/04/26, and the HUD disparate impact supplemental proposed rulemaking on 08/10/26. Long-term care and Medicare and Medicaid each shed one. Medicare and Medicaid remains the busiest beat by a wide margin, 26 items drawn from seven sources including ACL, CMS, the Federal Register, KFF and Justice in Aging, but its cohesion is 0.054 and the items share a tag and nothing else. It is not one story and should not be pitched as one. Long-term care is the opposite case: fewer items, 18, but they hold together at 0.256 around the 08/01/26 CMS provider data refresh, and that is where the assignable work is. Palliative and hospice care is the tightest cluster in the run at 0.457 across CMS and RAND, nine items, none matched by monitored publishers. Coverage posture is unusually open. There are 84 confirmed gaps, meaning beats we do watch where nobody matched the item, and another 76 items sit on beats no monitored publisher covers at all, which tells us nothing about whether they have been written elsewhere. The practical read: the federal data pipeline is doing the work this week, most of it is localizable to states and counties, and the competitive risk on the nursing home files is that they have been sitting in public since 08/01/26.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** On 08/01/26 CMS refreshed nearly the entire public record on nursing homes in a single sweep: Health Deficiencies, Fire Safety Deficiencies, Penalties, Ownership, Provider Information (the file behind the Five-Star Rating System), MDS Quality Measures, Survey Summary, Inspection Dates and the Citation Code Look-up, alongside Medicare Claims Quality Measures and the Skilled Nursing Facility Quality Reporting Program provider file. Every one of those carries state and county detail. Three other sources land on the same story inside the same window: BLS puts nursing care facilities employment at 1,590.20 thousand jobs in August 2026, up 2.1% year over year, while home health care services employment reached 1,896.40 thousand, up 5.0%; Justice in Aging's 08/20/26 primer on Medicaid home and community-based services describes the policy gaps that limit access to the community alternative; and the Center for Retirement Research on 09/03/26 sets the U.S. long-term care system against Israel's. The connective tissue is not "quality data" in the abstract. It is that the institutional side of long-term care is now documented down to the individual citation and the individual owner, refreshed this month, while the alternative most families would prefer stays rationed by program design and staffed by a workforce growing two and a half times faster than the facility workforce. Seventeen of the 18 items in this cluster went unmatched by the publishers we monitor.

**Why pitch this now:** Medicaid is the payer behind most of this care, and its financing is actively being rewritten. KFF's 08/20/26 brief describes how the rules governing state provider taxes are changing because of the 2025 reconciliation law and the regulations implementing it, and which states each change may affect. In the same weeks, HUD published FY 2027 fair market rents on 09/01/26 with an October 1 effective date and the Housing Trust Fund FY 2026 allocation notice on 09/04/26, both of which shape what the community alternative actually costs. Families make fall placement decisions against exactly this backdrop, and the facility-level record they need to make them was refreshed weeks ago with almost no one reading it out.

**Angle:** "What Your State's Nursing Homes Were Cited For," a state-by-state read of the 08/01/26 CMS refresh that pairs health and fire safety citations and penalties with ownership records and staffing measures, written for families comparing facilities now, with a companion trade cut on what the same files say about staffing and ownership concentration.

**Potential headlines:**
- Every nursing home citation in your state, updated last month
- The nursing home fines nobody read
- Who owns the nursing home you are about to choose

**Potential outlets:**
- Kiplinger, which handles long-term care costs and state comparisons for a retirement audience and can carry the consumer version of a 50-state build.
- SeniorLiving.org, a major consumer senior-living publisher that runs state rankings and data studies and would take the facility-comparison framing directly.
- Family Caregiver Alliance, the natural distribution partner for the version aimed at an adult child choosing a facility this month.
- McKnight's Long-Term Care News, the primary trade home for skilled nursing survey, citation and staffing data.
- Skilled Nursing News, for the ownership and penalties cut, where original data with business implications performs.
- Provider Magazine, strong on Medicaid, staffing and quality and well suited to state-by-state tables.
